description: We’re a team of six sixth-form students from Pate’s Grammar School, combining our interests in physics, mathematics and computer science to tackle real-world challenges through creative problem-solving and collaboration.
summary:
We developed an interactive lunar landing-site re-evaluation platform, integrating NASA LOLA topographic data with JPL ephemerides, for evidence-based mission planning after unexpected launch scrubs and re-schedules.


The platform combines interactive 3D terrain simulations, UTC-synchronised solar illumination and shadow modelling, and terrain-aware Earth line-of-sight analysis for communications assessment. Users can explore nine modelled lunar locations across eighteen 72-hour scenarios, shortlist candidate sites and compare their suitability through numerical metrics and visual graphs for full/partial/no sunlight, earth communication windows, sun-earth overlap and power-generation potential.


An integrated Learning Centre provides tutorials, scientific explanations and educational resources for technical and non-technical audiences. We took this further through a Gemini API that can interact with the site (however this was not fully implemented). We emphasised scientific traceability, with documented data sources, assumptions, uncertainties and exportable results.


Unlike existing tools focused on isolated terrain maps, ephemerides or basic solar-angle calculations, our platform unifies these capabilities into a decision-making conclusive workflow. Its differentiators are terrain-obstructed Solar / Earth visibility, synchronised 3D simulations, direct site  comparisons and interactive educational guidance, helping users evaluate sites and make evidence-based decisions.
details:
Our project was developed around a specific problem in lunar mission planning: what happens when a scheduled launch is delayed, and the original landing window is no longer favourable? A change in arrival time can significantly affect illumination, surface conditions and communication opportunities. We wanted to provide a practical way of reassessing these factors without requiring mission planners and also the public to operate several specialist and complex NASA tools to obtain the required result.

The platform follows a structured Catalogue, Explore, Compare workflow. Users can browse 36 cited lunar locations, identify those supported by numerical analysis, investigate their surrounding terrain and compare alternative landing windows. Behind the interface, Python scripts process NASA LOLA elevation datasets into regional terrain models and calculate local horizon profiles. JPL Horizons supplies the prepared Sun and Earth positions, which are evaluated against the terrain profiles rather than assuming an unobstructed horizon. The results are then organised into time-dependent visibility intervals, allowing users to investigate how conditions change throughout a scenario.

One important technical consideration was ensuring that datasets from different sources could be combined reliably. We had to account for coordinate systems, lunar reference frames, elevation measurements, UTC precision and the spatial resolution of terrain data. We also considered the computational demands of processing large elevation datasets. Rather than repeatedly downloading and analysing entire lunar maps, we prepared bounded terrain regions and reusable scientific results. These are delivered through a lightweight browser interface, with additional ephemeris queries supported through NASA/JPL WebGeocalc.

We developed the application primarily using TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML/CSS and Python. Three.js provides interactive 3D visualisation, while Rasterio and pyproj support terrain extraction and geospatial calculations. Node.js and esbuild handle application builds, with Cloudflare Pages, Functions and D1 supporting hosting, backend services and structured data storage. Development was coordinated through GitHub, using issues, pull requests, GitHub Actions and Playwright testing to manage implementation and verify functionality.

Our approach was also influenced by the limitations we identified in existing tools. QuickMap provides detailed lunar mapping, Moon Trek offers terrain visualisation and basic solar-angle information, and Horizons supplies precise ephemerides. However, using these independently requires substantial interpretation and manual comparison. We wanted to connect the scientific calculations directly to the process of selecting and comparing candidate sites, while making the reasoning behind each result understandable.

Accessibility and education were equally important considerations. The Learning Centre includes a guided application tutorial, scientific explanations and printable classroom investigations. We also explored integrating a Gemini-powered assistant for contextual explanations and interaction with the platform, although this feature was not fully completed. Our intention was to make the project useful beyond specialist mission planners, particularly for students, educators and the wider public interested in the Artemis programme.

Finally, we prioritised scientific transparency over presenting misleading precision. Each analysis retains its source references, assumptions, coverage limitations and unknown values. For example, geometric Earth visibility does not guarantee a working communications link, and our current analysis does not establish landing safety or complete mission feasibility.

The intended impact is twofold: to demonstrate how NASA datasets can be integrated into a more practical, evidence-based mission-planning process, and to make the scientific reasoning behind lunar landing-site decisions accessible to a much wider audience.
